summary: Provides a way to carry extra join and enrollment information in the Enhanced Beacon frames that announce a TSCH network. This helps new and long-sleeping nodes find and join the network, since broadcast opportunities are limited.

plainLanguage.summary: Beacons that announce a network now also carry tips for newcomers, because there are so few chances to broadcast.

questions: how do nodes learn join info in tsch
what is the 6tisch join info ie
what is a network id in 6tisch
how does a pledge pick a join proxy
subtitle: Extra join and enrollment hints packed into the beacon frames that announce a TSCH network.

tldr.problem: In a TSCH network, broadcast opportunities are rare. New nodes (pledges) and long-sleeping nodes would otherwise have to spend extra scarce broadcast slots on IPv6 router messages before they can join.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a new IETF Information Element subtype, carried inside the Enhanced Beacon, with a router flag, a join proxy priority and optional address, a rank priority, a PAN priority and a network ID.
tldr.outcome: A node learns what it needs to pick a network and a join proxy from the beacon alone. All of it is sent in the clear, so the RFC lists what an attacker can learn from each field.

today: RFC 9032 is a Proposed Standard from May 2021 and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It refers to RFC 9031 for the Join Proxy role, and RFC 9033 mentions this IE as one way to filter beacons when joining.

sections.title: The Problem: Scarce Broadcasts
sections.content:
In the Time-Slotted Channel Hopping (TSCH) mode of IEEE Std 802.15.4, broadcasts can only happen at specific times and on specific channels. Routers announce their network with Enhanced Beacon (EB) frames sent in broadcast slots. The RFC gives an example of 10 ms slots and a slotframe length of 100, which could leave only 1 slot per second for broadcasts, and that slot has to carry the beacon.

This document defines a new IETF Information Element (IE) subtype that is placed into the EB. It gives prospective pledges join and enrollment information more efficiently.
sections.plainLanguage: A shop that only opens its door for a moment each second cannot tell customers much. So the sign on the door should say as much as possible.

sections.title: Why Layer 2 and Layer 3 Discovery Is Costly
sections.content:
An EB carries synchronization information such as the Absolute Slot Number (ASN) and Join Metric, identifiers for the timeslot template and channel hopping sequence, and the TSCH slotframe. A pledge uses it to learn about and synchronize with the network.

At Layer 3, IPv6 nodes normally learn about routers from multicast Router Advertisements (RA). If none arrives, a node may send a Router Solicitation (RS). In a TSCH network this is expensive: there are few multicast timeslots, and an RS consumes a broadcast Aloha slot with unencrypted traffic. The RFC says a pledge might need many seconds of on-time to get an RA, and perhaps dozens of seconds or even minutes for each enrollment attempt if it must stay in receive state for an RA as well as find the EB.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking the whole room a question out loud wastes everyone's time. It is faster if the answer is already written on the name tag.

sections.title: The Join and Enrollment IE
sections.content:
RFC 8137 creates a registry for IETF IE subtypes, and this document allocates a new one. The length of the subtype content can be calculated from the container, so the structure has no length field. It holds these fields:

  • R: the RA R-flag, set if the sender will act as a router for host-only nodes that use SLAAC. Those hosts MUST send a unicast RS to receive an RA with the Prefix Information Option.
  • P: if set, the Join Proxy Interface ID field is present.
  • proxy prio: willingness to act as a Join Proxy. Lower means more willing, from 0x00 to 0x7e. A value of 0x7f means the sender should never be considered as a Join Proxy.
  • rank priority: set by the 6LR to show how willing it is to be a RPL parent. Pledges MUST ignore it.
  • PAN priority: set by the DODAG root, typically the 6LBR. Lower values mean more willingness to accept new nodes. Unenrolled pledges MAY consider it.
  • Join Proxy Interface ID: 64 bits (8 bytes) giving the interface ID of the proxy's link-local address (prefix fe80::/64). If absent, the ID is derived from the sender's Layer 2 address.
  • network ID: variable length, up to 16 bytes, filling the rest of the IE.

Reserved bits MUST be ignored on receipt and SHOULD be set to 0 when sending.
sections.plainLanguage: Each beacon carries a little card: am I a router, how happy am I to help newcomers, how busy is my group, and what is the name of my network.

sections.title: Choosing a Network and a Proxy
sections.content:
A large low-power network can consist of several Layer 2 instances called Personal Area Networks (PANs), joined by Backbone Routers. Each has its own PANID, a 16-bit value, and its own Layer 2 security profile. The new network ID tells which PANs belong to the same backbone: PANs in the same backbone are configured with the same network ID. Pledges that see the same network ID will not waste time trying to enroll several times with the same network.

As a suggested default, the network ID can be built from a truncated SHA-256 hash of the /64 prefix of the network, computed by the RPL DODAG root. It may be set in any convenient way that results in a non-identifying value. How the PAN priority is calculated is left to future work, and the rank priority is described as experimental.

A device that wakes from a long sleep can use the PAN priority and rank priority to pick a less congested PAN or one with a shallower RPL tree.
sections.plainLanguage: If a town has several train stations with the same line, the network ID says they belong together, and the priority says which one is least crowded.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Everything in this IE is sent in the clear because the EB is not encrypted. This is a restriction in the 802.15.4 cryptographic architecture, since the ASN is needed to decrypt or check Layer 2 frames and the EB is what provides the ASN. The EB is authenticated at Layer 2 with network-wide keying material, but pledges that have not enrolled cannot check it and must take the contents on faith until after enrollment.

Each field has its own leak. The R flag being unset may flag an under-provisioned node. Rank priority and PAN priority can point an attacker to busier nodes or PANs. The network ID lets an observer with a radio sniffer map the extent of a mesh, though hashing the DODAGID keeps the root address out of it. The TSCH schedule in the EB also tells an attacker which channels will be used, which can make jamming more efficient.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the sign is public, anyone walking by can read it, including people who want to cause trouble. So the RFC lists what each line gives away.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA assigned value 2, named 6tisch-Join-Info, in the "IEEE Std 802.15.4 IETF IE Subtype IDs" registry defined by RFC 8137. This is also the value shown in the first byte of the structure in the RFC's figure.
sections.plainLanguage: The new kind of note got its own number in the official list, so everybody can recognise it.

items.title: R and P flags
items.text: R: sender acts as a router for SLAAC hosts. P: a Join Proxy Interface ID follows.

items.title: proxy prio
items.text: 0x00 most willing to 0x7e least willing; 0x7f never a proxy.

items.title: rank priority
items.text: How willing a 6LR is to be a RPL parent. Pledges ignore it.

items.title: PAN priority
items.text: Set by the DODAG root. Lower means more willing to accept new nodes.

items.title: network ID
items.text: Variable length, up to 16 bytes, shared by PANs on one backbone.
